site-enhancement-oil-synthol.summary: Oil injected into a muscle to make it look bigger or reshaped right away; case reports describe embolism, granulomas, nerve damage and infection.

quick.overview:
Site enhancement oil (SEO), best known as Synthol, is an oily liquid injected into a muscle so it looks bigger or differently shaped. Bodybuilders use it on lagging or disproportionate areas such as biceps and delts, a practice called fluffing.

The change is visible straight away because the oil sits in the muscle as a deposit and distends it; it does not add muscle tissue. A commonly reported formulation is about 85% oil, 7.5% lidocaine and 7.5% alcohol, with sesame oil often used, and some people inject PMMA or paraffin oil instead. Published material is mostly case reports and short articles; no clinical trials were found.
quick.how: People use it on specific muscles they want to look fuller or more proportioned, usually as a repeated procedure over time rather than a one-off. It is mostly associated with competitive and professional bodybuilders and is typically paired with ordinary training. Injected muscle is described as not truly developed and may droop under gravity, so the size shows up at once but depends on the deposit staying in place.
quick.risks: Reported complications include pulmonary oil embolism, stroke, nerve damage, infection, oil-filled granulomas (sclerosing lipogranuloma), cysts, ulcers and allergic vasculitis from sesame oil; a 2011 case study described multi-organ dysfunction in a user of multiple substances. Synthol is not restricted and is sold online, while PMMA for muscle shaping is prohibited in the US. Anyone with allergies to the oils or a history of clotting or circulation problems faces added concern.

angle.text: Bodybuilders inject oil into lagging muscles such as biceps and delts to make them look bigger or reshape them. The size change shows straight away and comes from the oil volume, not new muscle tissue. Case reports document serious complications.

progressive-overload-hypertrophy-trainin.summary: Steadily adding weight, reps or sets so muscles keep adapting; the core method lifters use to build a bigger physique.

quick.overview:
Progressive overload means gradually raising the demand on your muscles by adding weight, repetitions, sets or other stress. It is the standard approach lifters use to build a bigger, more muscular physique.

The chain: training under greater-than-normal demand first drives neural adaptation, then increases in muscle mass and connective-tissue strength. Mechanical tension is the currently accepted theory of hypertrophy, activating mTOR signaling and muscle protein synthesis. Research links hypertrophy to mechanical tension, training volume and progressive overload, and the best ways to apply it are still being studied.
quick.how: Lifters log their sessions and nudge up load, reps or sets over weeks and months, usually inside a routine or split. Periodization is used to plan harder and easier phases. Visible muscle gain builds over months of consistent training, alongside enough food and recovery.
quick.risks: Excessive training can cause overtraining, which periodization is used to help manage. Injury risk depends on technique, load and individual factors. Increasing load too fast or with breaking form is the usual way people get hurt.

angle.text: Lifters add weight or reps over time so muscles keep adapting, which is how a bigger physique gets built. Training demand drives muscle protein synthesis and, over months, more muscle. It is widely taught in strength science, with the details of how best to progress still studied.

push-pull-legs-ppl.summary: A three-way weekly lifting split of push, pull and leg days that lets you train each muscle about twice a week to build physique.

quick.overview:
Push/pull/legs, or PPL, divides weekly weight training into a push day (chest, shoulders, triceps), a pull day (back, biceps) and a leg day. It is one of several common splits alongside full-body, upper/lower and the bro split, and lifters use it to build a muscular physique.

A split spreads weekly training volume across muscle groups and days. Run twice through a week, PPL hits each muscle about twice. Research summarised on Wikipedia reports that with equal volume, frequency did not change strength gains, and for muscle growth two sessions per week produced greater effects than one. No comparative research on PPL versus other splits is cited.
quick.how: People run it as three days on a rotating schedule or as six days a week, with rest days placed where recovery needs them. It is commonly paired with progressive overload and a calorie surplus when the goal is size. Visible changes build over months.
quick.risks: No harms specific to PPL are documented. General resistance-training cautions apply, such as overtraining from excessive volume, and the six-day version leaves less rest time between sessions.

angle.text: A popular weekly split for building a muscular physique, with each muscle trained about twice a week across push, pull and leg days. More frequent work per muscle spreads volume across the week toward steady growth. Research on frequency shows two weekly sessions produced greater muscle growth than one.

bro-split.summary: A weekly routine that trains one muscle group per day with high volume, a classic bodybuilding way to build size.

quick.overview:
The bro split gives each session to one muscle group, for example chest one day, then back, shoulders, arms and legs. It is a classic bodybuilding arrangement for building size and is widely used in gym culture.

Each muscle gets a lot of volume in one session and is trained directly about once per week. Research summarised on Wikipedia says two sessions per week per muscle produced greater muscle growth than one, while with equal volume frequency did not influence strength. No comparative research ranking the bro split against other splits is cited.
quick.how: Lifters assign a body part to each weekday and do many exercises and sets for that muscle in the session, usually with the weekend off. It is often combined with progressive overload and a surplus when size is the goal. Results build over months.
quick.risks: No harms specific to the bro split are documented. General resistance-training cautions apply, including overtraining with excessive volume and soreness from long single-muscle sessions.

angle.text: A classic bodybuilding routine that hits one muscle group hard each day to build size. High volume per session is the route to growth. Frequency research found two sessions per week per muscle produced greater growth than one.

beginner-strength-programs-5x5-ss-gzclp.summary: Linear-progression barbell routines that new lifters use to add strength and size quickly with a few compound lifts.

quick.overview:
Programs such as 5x5 (including StrongLifts), Starting Strength and GZCLP are barbell routines built on a few compound lifts: squat, bench press, overhead press and deadlift. New lifters use them as the usual starting point for building muscle and strength.

The load goes up by a small fixed amount each session or week, which authors say suits novices because they recover fast enough for steady progress, producing rapid early strength gains and then more muscle and better proportions. The programs come from coaches' books and websites; the wider research literature supports progressive resistance training generally, and no trials compare the named programs against each other.
quick.how: Lifters repeat the same few lifts several times a week and add a little weight each session until progress slows. Starting Strength is from Mark Rippetoe and Lon Kilgore's 2005 book and adds the power clean; GZCLP is a tiered template shared online. Many people follow one for the first months, then move to a split.
quick.risks: Heavy barbell lifting carries the usual resistance-training risks, mainly from poor technique or rapid load increases. No program-specific injury data were identified.

angle.text: Beginners follow these barbell programs to add size and strength quickly with a few compound lifts. Small load increases each session drive fast novice gains, which build muscle and improve frame and proportions. They are widely used and come from coaches' books and online templates.

high-intensity-training-hit-mentzer.summary: Mentzer's Heavy Duty and HIT: one or a few sets taken to failure with long rests, a time-efficient route to muscle size.

quick.overview:
High-intensity training (HIT) uses short, infrequent workouts with each set taken to momentary muscular failure. Arthur Jones, founder of Nautilus, popularised it in the 1970s, and bodybuilder Mike Mentzer developed his Heavy Duty version with very few sets and long recovery.

Followers argue muscle growth depends on intensity of effort rather than the amount of work, so a few all-out sets plus several days of recovery produce growth in far less gym time. Critics dispute its claims and its departure from conventional guidance. Sources describe the history and principles; no trials of Mentzer's complete system were found.
quick.how: Trainees do one or a few sets per exercise with slow, strict form until no more reps are possible, then rest several days before training that muscle again. Sessions are brief and total weekly volume is low compared with other bodybuilding routines.
quick.risks: Training to failure carries the general risks of resistance training, including fatigue and injury if form breaks down. No program-specific harm data were identified.

angle.text: Followers of Mentzer's Heavy Duty build muscle with brief, infrequent sessions taken to failure, then long recovery. Proponents say intensity of effort drives growth, so size comes with far less volume. It is a famous bodybuilding system, though the full protocol has not been tested as a whole.

renaissance-periodization-rp-volume-trai.summary: Mike Israetel's MEV/MAV/MRV framework for choosing weekly sets per muscle, popular with lifters planning efficient muscle growth.

quick.overview:
Renaissance Periodization (RP) is a coaching company founded in 2012 by Mike Israetel and Nick Shaw. Its best-known idea is three weekly volume landmarks for each muscle: minimum effective volume (MEV), maximum adaptive volume (MAV) and maximum recoverable volume (MRV).

The aim is to stay between the minimum that produces growth and the most you can recover from, so every set earns its place. The framework is widely discussed in lifting communities; Israetel is an exercise scientist and bodybuilder with a PhD in sports physiology. Independent efficacy studies of the full system were not found, and the figures come largely from RP's own material.
quick.how: Lifters start a training block near the low end of weekly sets per muscle, add sets as recovery allows, then reduce volume before repeating. RP also sells coaching, apps, courses and ebooks built on the system.
quick.risks: Higher volumes carry the general overuse and fatigue risks of resistance training. Critics mention cost and some diet recommendations; no system-specific harm data were identified.

angle.text: Lifters use the MEV, MAV and MRV framework to set how many weekly sets each muscle gets, aiming to stay between the minimum that works and the most they can recover from. Planning volume this way is meant to make muscle growth more efficient. It is popular in lifting circles, and no independent trial of the system itself was found.

blood-flow-restriction-bfr-training.summary: Cuff-assisted light-load lifting that builds muscle with less joint stress, with a real research base in rehab and sport.

quick.overview:
Blood flow restriction (BFR) training places a cuff or band on the upper arm or thigh to partly limit blood flow while you exercise with light loads. The payoff is muscle growth without heavy weights, with less joint stress. It originated in Japan in 1966 with Dr. Yoshiaki Sato as KAATSU.

The cuff mainly restricts blood leaving the muscle, creating a low-oxygen, metabolite-rich state that researchers think signals growth even at light loads. A 2012 meta-analysis and later reviews report strength and muscle-size gains from low-load BFR, with varied results across groups; a 2019 position stand covered methodology and safety. Forum claims linking it to height growth have not been studied. On forums BFR also often means buccal fat removal; this entry is the exercise method.
quick.how: People wrap the cuffs on the arms or legs during light sets, often as an add-on for sessions where heavy loading is hard, such as injury rehab or deloads. Used alongside normal training, gains build over weeks.
quick.risks: Reported effects include numbness, soreness and bruising; rare serious events such as rhabdomyolysis and thrombosis are described, especially with improvised straps. Clotting disorders and peripheral artery disease are listed contraindications.

angle.text: Users wrap cuffs on arms or legs so light weights stimulate muscle growth with less joint stress. Restricted blood outflow creates a metabolite-rich state in the muscle that researchers think triggers growth. It has a substantial rehab and sports research base, while forum claims about height gain have not been studied.

lengthened-partials-stretch-training.summary: Training the stretched part of each rep, such as the bottom of a curl or fly, to build more muscle in the target area.

quick.overview:
Lengthened partials are repetitions done only through the stretched portion of a lift, for example the bottom half of a curl or fly. Lifters use them to load the muscle where it is most elongated and get more growth in that muscle.

Hypertrophy overviews report that full range of motion, especially at elongated muscle lengths, is described as enhancing growth more than partial range, and that partial-range training at longer muscle lengths is also said to promote hypertrophy, possibly through muscle damage. The sources consulted do not summarise dedicated trials of lengthened partials.
quick.how: Lifters add them as extra reps at the end of a set or as the main way of performing exercises that load the muscle hard when stretched, such as curls, flyes and calf raises. They are used within a normal split and progressive overload plan.
quick.risks: Heavy loading in stretched positions can stress joints and connective tissue, as with other resistance training. No technique-specific harm data were identified.

angle.text: Lifters train only the stretched part of a rep, such as the bottom of a curl or fly, to build more muscle in that area. Keeping tension high when the muscle is elongated is thought to raise the growth stimulus. Hypertrophy overviews describe training at long muscle lengths as promoting growth, though dedicated trials are not summarised here.

myo-reps-drop-sets.summary: Time-saving to-failure set techniques that pack extra hard reps into shorter workouts for muscle growth.

quick.overview:
Drop sets and myo-reps are intensity techniques that pack more hard repetitions into less time so you get more muscle-building work per minute. A drop set keeps going with a lighter weight after failure at a heavier one; myo-reps use one high-effort set followed by several short mini-sets with brief rests.

Both keep the muscle working near failure for more total reps in a short window, which advocates say raises the growth stimulus per minute. Drop sets have a long history: Henry Atkins described the multi-poundage system in the late 1940s and they were part of Joe Weider's system in the 1980s. Coverage says drop sets may increase muscle growth more than traditional three-set training, while some researchers report mixed findings; a 2026 trial compared myo-reps with straight sets in resistance-trained men.
quick.how: Lifters tack them on to the last set of an exercise or use them for isolation moves when time is short. They are used inside a normal split alongside heavier compound work.
quick.risks: Working to failure adds fatigue and soreness, and general resistance-training injury risks apply. No technique-specific harm data were identified.

angle.text: Lifters use drop sets and myo-reps to pack more hard reps into less time, so shorter workouts still give a strong growth stimulus. Drop sets go back to the 1940s and may add growth compared with traditional sets, with some mixed findings. Myo-reps were only recently compared with straight sets in a trial.

shoulder-width-training-lateral-raises-d.summary: Building the side delts, mostly with lateral raises, to make your shoulders look wider and your frame more V-shaped.

quick.overview:
Shoulder-width training grows the deltoid muscles, especially the side (lateral) heads, so the shoulders look broader. Wider-looking shoulders improve upper-body proportions and feed the broad, V-shaped frame many people aim for.

The deltoid has three heads running from the clavicle and shoulder blade to the upper arm, and the middle fibers are best placed to lift the arm out to the side, which is what a lateral raise trains. Growing that muscle adds soft-tissue thickness at the sides of the shoulder, increasing measured and apparent width; the bone underneath stays as it is. Forum members post bideltoid measurements and compare them with height. No studies test shoulder-width training as an appearance intervention, though a small body of research looks at male shoulder dimensions and perceived attractiveness in general.
quick.how: The usual tool is the lateral raise, trained alongside presses and rows within a regular split, often several times a week. Visible change comes over months of consistent training and is easier to see at lower body fat.
quick.risks: Lifting carries ordinary training risks such as shoulder strain, and forum users joke about rotator cuff damage from very high volume. Muscle adds visible width but does not change skeletal shoulder width.

angle.text: Users train the side delts, mostly with lateral raises, to make the shoulders look wider and the frame more V-shaped. Bigger lateral deltoids add soft-tissue width at the top of the torso. Forum members post bideltoid measurements against height, and muscle changes visible width but not bone width.

v-taper-shoulder-to-waist-ratio.summary: The broad-shoulders, narrow-waist silhouette that lifters aim for, usually quoted as a shoulder-to-waist ratio near 1.6.

quick.overview:
A V-taper is a torso wide at the shoulders and upper back that narrows to a small waist, giving an inverted-triangle silhouette. It is a long-standing bodybuilding ideal and a standard frame goal in looksmaxxing, often written as a shoulder-to-waist ratio of about 1.6, tied to the golden ratio.

The ratio rises when the shoulders and upper back get wider or the waist gets smaller. Wider comes from deltoid and latissimus growth on top of the bone structure set by the clavicles; a smaller waist is mainly linked to body fat loss, and abdominal exercise alone is described as not enough to reduce waist girth. The 1.6 figure comes from bodybuilding culture; Wikipedia's waist-hip ratio article reports one study in which waist-to-chest ratio was the largest determinant of male attractiveness, and no studies of shoulder-to-waist ratio as a target were found.
quick.how: People train delts and lats, often with lateral raises, pull-ups and rows, while cutting body fat to narrow the waist. They track the ratio with a tape measure. Changes build over months of lifting and dieting.
quick.risks: The practice itself is ordinary training and dieting. Reported concerns are body-image fixation and skipping legs or overtraining while chasing a number. The 1.6 target is a cultural convention.

angle.text: Lifters and looksmaxxers aim for a shoulder-to-waist ratio near 1.6 by building the shoulders and back while cutting waist fat, producing an inverted-triangle silhouette. Muscle widens the top while fat loss narrows the middle. The 1.6 target is a forum and bodybuilding figure rather than a result from a specific attractiveness study.

biacromial-clavicle-width.summary: The bone-based width of your shoulder girdle, which looksmaxxers treat as the frame that muscle adds to.

quick.overview:
Biacromial width is the span across the acromion processes of the shoulder blades, and clavicle length is the length of the collarbones. Looksmaxxers use both to understand how wide the shoulders can look: muscle adds width on top of this skeletal base but does not change it.

The clavicle is an S-shaped bone lying horizontally between the sternum and shoulder blade. Males usually have longer and larger clavicles than females, and the bone finishes ossifying around age 21 to 25. Forum threads compare measurements and ask what counts as a high-status bideltoid number, often in inches at a stated height. These are community conventions; no studies of the measurements as appearance targets were found.
quick.how: People measure their shoulders and collarbones with a tape or in photos, then use the numbers to judge how much room delt and lat training has to add width. It is a measuring concept rather than a routine.
quick.risks: Measuring is harmless, though comparing numbers online can feed body-image concern. Surgery to alter the clavicle is a separate topic with its own risks, covered in the clavicle lengthening osteotomy article.

angle.text: Looksmaxxers treat biacromial and clavicle width as the fixed skeletal base that sets how wide the shoulders can look, with muscle adding soft-tissue width on top. Specific bideltoid numbers are quoted in forums as marks of a high-status frame. Those thresholds come from forum discussion rather than studies.

clavicle-lengthening-osteotomy.summary: A rare, extreme surgery discussed in hardmaxxing circles to widen the shoulders by cutting and lengthening the collarbones.

quick.overview:
Clavicle lengthening osteotomy is a surgical idea in which a collarbone is cut and lengthened to widen the shoulder span and give a broader-looking frame. In looksmaxxing it appears as an extreme, rarely performed hardmaxxing option and is not an established cosmetic operation.

An osteotomy is a surgical cut through bone; applied to the clavicle, the aim would be more bone length and so more shoulder breadth. Related operations in the surgical literature treat painful non-union and malunion after fractures. No studies or trials of clavicle lengthening for cosmetic widening were found, and registered clavicle trials concern fracture treatment, plates and pins.
quick.how: It is discussed as a rare option by people looking at skeletal changes that muscle cannot make. It would be done by a surgeon under anesthesia, which often involves nerve blocks, with recovery from bone surgery.
quick.risks: Clavicle surgery sits close to nerves and vessels. A published case series of operations for late fracture complications lists conditions such as thoracic outlet syndrome and brachial plexus neuroma among the problems treated. Anesthesia for clavicle surgery often involves nerve blocks that can affect breathing muscles.

angle.text: Hardmaxxing circles discuss cutting and lengthening the collarbones as an extreme way to widen the shoulder span and broaden the frame. It is raised as a rare option rather than an established cosmetic operation. The surgical literature on the clavicle concerns fractures and their complications.

stomach-vacuum-waist-training.summary: Pulling the belly in to train the deep abdominal muscle for a tighter, smaller-looking waist.

quick.overview:
The stomach vacuum is an exercise in which the abdomen is drawn inward, aimed at the transversus abdominis, the deepest of the four front abdominal wall muscles. Users practice it for a tighter abdominal wall and a smaller-looking waist that supports a V-taper.

The muscle is well described anatomically, but evidence on this use is thin: a looksmax.org thread has a user reporting he nearly lost the ability to do it and regained it with renewed training. Wikipedia notes it is disputed whether training this deep core muscle specifically is worthwhile, and a 2011 study found abdominal exercise alone does not reduce abdominal fat or girth.
quick.how: People practice it as a hold, drawing the belly in toward the spine, usually fitted into a warm-up or daily routine alongside regular training and fat loss. Waist training is sometimes also used for compression garments, which this entry does not cover.
quick.risks: No harms data were found for the exercise itself.

angle.text: Users practice the stomach vacuum to train the transversus abdominis and make the waist look smaller, supporting a V-taper. The muscle is well described anatomically. Research on this use is thin, and abdominal exercise alone does not reduce belly fat or girth according to a 2011 study.

neckmaxxing-neck-training.summary: Training the neck muscles for a thicker neck that looks more masculine and balances the jaw and frame.

quick.overview:
Neckmaxxing is training the neck muscles to make the neck thicker, which proponents say gives a more masculine, dominant look and better balance between the head, jaw and body. It is described on looksmax.org as a softmaxx.

Neck exercises load the muscles around the cervical spine, with the sternocleidomastoid named in forum guides as the muscle that thickens the neck from the front. Forum posts offer ratio targets, such as neck width to bigonial (jaw) width near 1:1 or a neck-to-height ratio near 1.35, and say a wider neck makes a narrow head and jaw look more in proportion. These are community conventions; no published study validates them and no clinical studies of neck training for appearance were found.
quick.how: People follow forum guides using neck curls, extensions and similar loaded movements added to a lifting routine, and track neck width with a tape. A thicker neck builds over months of consistent training.
quick.risks: Loaded neck exercises sit near the cervical spine, and one forum guide calls neck work one of the most dangerous softmaxxes. Gradual loading and careful form are the usual precautions in guides.

angle.text: Neckmaxxers train the neck to make it thicker, which they say adds a masculine, dominant look and better face and frame proportions. A wider neck sits more in balance with the jaw and shoulders. Neck-to-jaw ratio targets circulate on forums, and no published study validates them.

grip-and-forearm-training.summary: Targeted work for the hands and forearms to build grip strength and forearm size, popular for thicker-looking arms.

quick.overview:
Grip and forearm training exercises the muscles that close the hand and move the wrist, with wrist curls, dead hangs, loaded carries and grippers. In looksmaxxing and physique circles it is used for bigger forearms, which posters describe as part of a strong, masculine arm and wrist look.

The forearm has a front (flexor) group that flexes the wrist and fingers, a back (extensor) group, muscles that rotate the forearm, and the brachioradialis, an elbow flexor. Training loads these muscles so they adapt as other muscles do under resistance. Published studies, mostly in athletes or lab settings, include a 4-week unilateral forearm trial that increased endurance time, 12-week programs in high school baseball players and a hybrid method that reported gains in forearm strength and mass in healthy men. No study examines perceived attractiveness, and wrist circumference and bone structure are described as unchanged by training.
quick.how: Lifters add a few forearm and grip exercises at the end of arm or back workouts, or build grip through hangs and carries. Strength sports also treat grip as a performance factor in pulling lifts. Size gains build over weeks to months.
quick.risks: Forearm training is generally low-risk exercise. Overuse of the wrist and elbow tendons is a general concern with repetitive loading.

angle.text: Lifters use wrist curls, hangs, carries and grippers to build forearm size and grip strength, valued for thicker, more muscular-looking arms. Loading the forearm muscles makes them adapt like other muscles. Published trials mostly measure strength, endurance or size, not how attractive the result looks.

calisthenics-gymnast-physique.summary: Bodyweight training with push-ups, pull-ups and dips to build a lean, broad-shouldered gymnast-style physique with little equipment.

quick.overview:
Calisthenics is strength training that uses body weight as resistance: push-ups, pull-ups, dips, squats, planks and advanced skills such as handstands, levers and the planche. The payoff is the gymnast physique, a lean, muscular upper body with wide shoulders and a narrow waist, built at low cost with little or no equipment.

Muscle is loaded by moving through harder variations, more repetitions or slower tempos, which is progressive overload, and proponents say this produces hypertrophy similar to weight training in beginners. Posters disagree about whether it matches weights for muscle size, particularly in the legs. No trial found tests calisthenics for physique or perceived attractiveness; related research mostly uses it as a comparison arm.
quick.how: People train at home, in parks or on pull-up bars with routines built around pull-ups, chin-ups, push-ups, dips and squats, moving to harder variations as they get stronger. Progress toward a visible physique builds over months.
quick.risks: Calisthenics is generally low-cost and low-risk, though advanced skills place heavy loads on the wrists, elbows and shoulders.

angle.text: People use push-ups, pull-ups, dips and skills like levers to build a lean, muscular, gymnast-style body with little equipment. Progressively harder bodyweight variations drive muscle gain while body fat stays low. Bodyweight training is studied for strength and muscle, and trials of its aesthetic results are not found.

ring-training-planche-progressions.summary: Gymnastic-style strength work on rings and planche holds, a skill-based route to a bigger, gymnast-like upper body.

quick.overview:
Ring training uses suspended gymnastic rings for push, pull and hold exercises, and the planche is a straight-arm hold with the body horizontal above the hands. Practitioners use them to build the broad, muscular upper body of a gymnast.

The rings are unstable, so the body must control the movement as well as lift it, and progressions move from easier variations toward the full skill by adjusting leverage. Both come from gymnastics and calisthenics; Wikipedia describes the planche as the most advanced of the common calisthenics skills, often reached only after years of training. No published study tests ring or planche training for appearance outcomes.
quick.how: People hang a pair of rings from a bar or frame and work through ring dips, rows, pushups and leaning hold progressions, building toward holds over months to years. It is usually done alongside other calisthenics or lifting.
quick.risks: Advanced straight-arm static holds load the wrists, elbows and shoulders heavily.

angle.text: Practitioners use ring dips, levers and planche progressions as a skill-based route to upper-body size and a gymnast look. Unstable rings and leverage-based progressions load the muscles hard, building a broader upper body. No studies of appearance outcomes were found.

dirty-bulk-lean-bulk.summary: Two ways of eating in a calorie surplus to gain size: a large, loosely tracked surplus or a small, controlled one, usually followed by a cut.

quick.overview:
Bulking means eating in a calorie surplus to build muscle, usually followed by a cutting phase in a deficit that reveals the new size. A lean (clean) bulk uses a small, tracked surplus to limit fat gain; a dirty bulk uses a large, loosely tracked surplus that can include processed foods, giving faster weight gain.

A surplus supplies energy for tissue growth. Wikipedia says a sustained surplus can add more lean mass than eating at maintenance, with some fat gain expected, and a larger surplus or longer bulk adds more fat. Competitive bodybuilders spend most of the year building and cut for roughly 12 to 14 weeks before a contest. On looksmax.org, thinner users ask which approach avoids looking soft or bloated, and no trial tests clean versus dirty bulking for appearance.
quick.how: Lifters raise their calories while training with progressive overload, track weight and measurements, and cut once they reach the size they want. Lean bulkers keep the surplus small and watch the scale; dirty bulkers eat freely and accept a longer cut afterward.
quick.risks: Wikipedia describes dirty bulking as producing fast gain but usually significant fat, followed by a harsher cut, with long-term concerns for cardiovascular health and insulin sensitivity. Forum users also report fear of looking fat or bloated.

angle.text: Lifters eat in a calorie surplus to fuel muscle growth, either a large loosely tracked one (dirty bulk) or a small controlled one (lean bulk), then cut to reveal the size. More energy means more lean mass, with a larger surplus adding more fat. The practice comes from bodybuilding, and forum posters debate which style looks best.
